What is a parasite, anyway?

Before the specimens — the definitions, the categories, and the strange range of things "parasite" actually covers.

A parasite lives on or inside another organism — its host — drawing nourishment or shelter at the host's expense. Unlike a predator, which kills quickly, most parasites keep their host alive as long as possible: a dead host is a home lost. Biologists sort that basic relationship several different ways.

Ectoparasites vs. Endoparasites

Ectoparasites live on the outside of a host — lice, ticks, or Cymothoa exigua gripping a fish's tongue. Endoparasites live inside it — tapeworms in an intestine, flukes in a blood vessel.

Obligate vs. Facultative

Obligate parasites, like Toxoplasma gondii, cannot complete their life cycle without a host at all. Facultative parasites can survive independently but will exploit a host if the opportunity arises.

Direct vs. Indirect Life Cycles

A direct cycle needs only one host, like Taenia solium moving from pig to person. An indirect (complex) cycle needs two or more — an intermediate host where the parasite develops, and a definitive host where it reproduces.

Parasitoids & Hyperparasites

Parasitoids, like the wasps in this guide, develop inside a host and eventually kill it — part predator, part parasite. A hyperparasite, like Gelis agilis, goes a step further: it parasitizes another parasite.

Intermediate vs. Definitive Hosts

An intermediate host is where a parasite develops or multiplies asexually. A definitive host is where it reaches adulthood and reproduces sexually — the destination the whole life cycle is built around.

Parasites Aren't Just Animals

Fungi (Ophiocordyceps), single-celled protozoa (Toxoplasma), and plants (Cuscuta, Ficus) all evolved parasitic strategies independently. Some biologists estimate parasitic species may outnumber free-living ones — parasitism isn't an edge case in nature, it's one of its dominant strategies.

TAKE ACTION

Fighting back.

Parasites are part of every healthy ecosystem — but when one turns up somewhere new, or a preventable infection spreads unchecked, there's real value in knowing what actually helps.

What happens if we don't act

Not a forecast for any single species — but the trajectory the real data points toward if the trends underlying it continue.

37,000+ and climbing

Over 37,000 alien species have already been introduced worldwide by human activity, and a "business as usual" path is projected to add 36% more by 2050.

60% of extinctions

Invasive alien species have played a role in roughly 60% of global plant and animal extinctions recorded — and were the sole cause in about 16% of them.

90% of island losses

On islands specifically — exactly the kind of isolated place sea lampreys and Toxoplasma-carrying cats reached — invasive species have driven roughly 90% of recorded extinctions.

Cost quadrupling every decade

The global economic toll of invasive species passed $423 billion a year in 2019 — and has roughly quadrupled each decade since 1970. Left unmanaged, that curve doesn't flatten on its own.

Source: IPBES Assessment Report on Invasive Alien Species and their Control (2023) — the most comprehensive global review to date, compiled by 86 experts from 49 countries.
